rv.q: I defy anyone not to fall in love with it.
Complex ideas about love, literature, body image and truth are expressed in its dizzyingly clever rhymes, but essentially it remains a captivating, tragicomic romance.
There is nothing fey or decorative.

I feel more sure of myself in declaring the show – which kicks off a season of Jamie Lloyd productions at the Playhouse that includes Jessica Chastain’s West End debut in Ibsen’s A Doll’s House – inspired in its minimalist eloquence.
Yes there are times when Lloyd's production feels like it's striving too hard to generate a hip, post-Hamilton vibe, but it tempers this with a sense of humour.

Lloyd’s production makes you see an old play with fresh eyes and the opening image, in Soutra Gilmour’s stark design, of Cyrano staring fixedly at himself in a mirror, turns Rostand’s comedy into a study in physical and linguistic self-regard.
This time, McAvoy comes up with a breathtaking career-best performance, and the entire evening is a dazzling triumph.
It is a triumph, a breathtakingly bold rethinking of a classic in resonant contemporary ways.
I wouldn't necessarily want all my classics to be delivered in this way, but Lloyd's company is committed to attracting a youthful audience.

cn.t: Jamie Lloyd's radical, stripped-down Cyrano wows critics with James McAvoy's electrifying performance and Martin Crimp's modern verse adaptation, though some question the lack of prosthetic nose and bold departures from tradition.
